chapter: Georgie Auld, Hawkins and Los Angeles
title: Hawkins' tightness, leaving, and the union blocking Billy Berg's
summary: Hawkins refuses a raise, McGhee stays in California, and union officials stop him from returning to Billy Berg's with his own band until payoffs clear the way.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: But like, I mentioned before money, you know. Hawk was a tight son of a gun, boy. He didn't believe in giving up a quarter. So I told him, I said, "Look, Hawk, I think I deserve a raise. I know all your tunes you're playing, and I can play," and you know... So he had different ideas. He figured, "Oh, well, I can get Joe Guy." So I said, "Well, if you can get Joe Guy, maybe you'd better get him, because I don't think I'm going back to New York. Not right now anyway. I want to stay out here awhile."

So after we come out of Billy Berg's, the union man told me, "Well, you know you can't go in Billy Berg's" -- because he'd heard I was rehearsing the band, you know. So he said, "You know you can't come out of one job and go right back in there with your own band. We don't allow that out here." I said, "Oh no? Well, okay." So in the meantime, Billy Berg called me up and said, "Hey, are you coming in?" I said, "Well, the union man told me I couldn't come in." He says, "Oh, don't worry about them. I'll fix that." I said, "Oh yeah?" That really pulled my eyes open to what was happening with the social activities of California.
But then shortly the cat called me back, and said... in

the meantime, the lady from San Diego had called me and asked me would I come down there and play, because she'd heard I was getting a band together. So I said, "Well, sure, I'll come down. I have no commitments."

That was in San Diego, at some club down there that this lady was promoting. Anyway, what's that guy's name....Brady called me from the union, and told me that it was all right if I wanted to go in and play Billy Berg's. But then a couple of hours before, they'd told me I couldn't do it. So I seen who was running what, you know. I said, "Oh yeah, mmm-hmm."
Shove a couple of dollars in the right hand...

Yeah, it cleared the way. Well, Billy Berg didn't have to do nothing. He just called up down there and told them he wanted me to come in, and they said "Okay" to him, but they told me, no, you couldn't do this.

And Elmer Fain was one of the big union executives. He was telling me, he said, "Well, if the man wanted to hire you, I don't understand why you don't take it." I said, "Well, I've got another job to go on to now, and I've got to live up to that." So he said, "Oh, you don't want to go in

Billy Berg's?" I said, "Not particularly, no. I played there. I just come out of there. I've been there eight weeks. Now I'm going down to San Diego. I'm going to play for..." I can't think of the lady's name; "I'm going to play for her."
